title: The clever sage
hook: Mahosadha solves the court's riddles and saves the kingdom by wit (Jataka 546)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vidhura the pandita, a wise one, who taught the spirit carrying him off. Your line: he taught his captor. Today, a boy who solves things.

Two women, one baby, and a judge who is still a child. Each woman swears the baby is hers. Nobody saw what happened. In the Jataka the judge is a village boy named Mahosadha, who has built a hall where people bring their quarrels, and this is one of them. He doesn't ask for witnesses. He draws a line on the ground.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE BABY.` → `A BOY JUDGE.` → `A LINE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The story says he was born holding a healing herb, and so he was called Mahosadha, great medicine: a fitting name for someone whose gift is fixing things. Back to the line. He places the baby on it and tells the women to pull, one by the arms, one by the legs; whoever pulls the child across keeps him. They pull. The baby cries out. And one woman lets go, rather than hurt him. That, the boy says, is the mother. The other, the story reveals, wasn't human at all. Case after case goes like that: he finds the answer by watching how people act, not by guessing. Word reaches King Vedeha of Mithila, who brings the boy to court. There, jealous advisers test him, scheme against him, try to get him thrown out. He keeps answering riddles, keeps seeing through traps. When a rival king threatens Mithila, Mahosadha's plan, a great tunnel, the ummagga the tale is named for, turns a trap into a peace and saves his king. Tradition pairs this tale with wisdom, panna. It's a practical wisdom. It reads people, and it's always used to protect someone: the baby, the cheated, the king. The baby goes home with the woman who let go.
screen: `BORN HOLDING A HEALING HERB.` · `THE MOTHER LETS GO.` · `RIDDLES AND TRAPS AT COURT.` · `A GREAT TUNNEL SAVES THE KING.` · then, large: `WIT THAT SAVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose mood you've been guessing at lately, a child, a coworker, a friend who's gone quiet. Set the guesses aside and recall only what they actually did this week, what they reached for and when they lit up, and let their actions tell you something, the way the mother's letting go told Mahosadha.
Panna. Wisdom: what Mahosadha the boy judge showed, reading people well and using his wit to protect them, all the way to saving his king. Today's word.
Your line: wit that saves. His cleverness always worked for someone else. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Mahosadha story is told as a tale of practical wisdom; in Buddhist teaching, wisdom (panna) is one of the ten perfections.

chat.says: How did the boy judge know which woman was the real mother?

He asked the neighbors, who had seen the baby being born.

chat.meaning: Mahosadha read people by what they did. The true mother let go rather than hurt the child.

Mahosadha.meaning: the boy judge, named great medicine

Vedeha.meaning: the king of Mithila who brought the boy to court

ummagga.meaning: a tunnel; the tale is named for one

Confirm the traditional pairing Mahosadha = panna (wisdom).
The child case resembles stories in other traditions; deliberately not compared.
